rows.source: LeCun & Balestriero, "Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPA" (29 Oct), via MindStudio's write-up
rows.claim: A learned world model that predicts in an abstract representation space rather than raw pixels or words, so it can ignore unpredictable detail; it must be kept from "collapse" (one generic summary for everything); "good views" (different observations of the same event) push models towards shared structure. A ~109M-parameter JEPA model reportedly beat models up to 72B on one world-understanding benchmark
rows.evidence: One paper, one benchmark, read through a vendor blog
rows.done: Poesys's world is an explicit simulation of the GB record behind the wall, not a learned model. Three parallels, filed under the abstraction family (7 Nov steer): (1) model each thing at the level it is predictable, which is how the world is fitted to aggregates; (2) collapse is our averaging failure, one measure across distinct populations (bill shock, average unit rate), which the register's one-definition-per-measure must not reproduce by merging distinct concepts; (3) good views is triangulation, a claim held by two independent observations (world claims against published data) rather than one. Also E-08 in the director's 5 Nov research pack

rows.source: An AI-written research summary the director shared: "AI delegation fails from uncurated context", citing Ehsani et al. (arXiv 2601.15195), Microsoft's delegation-failure taxonomy, a "verification scarcity" paper and the Glean Work AI Index
rows.claim: Silent, low-noticeability failures burn the overseer's attention; agent PR failures spike across module boundaries; the bottleneck is verification, not generation. Four rules: distil sub-agent output, map code before writing, deterministic hard gates, machine-readable boundaries
rows.evidence: Mixed: Ehsani and the Microsoft taxonomy are real; the "verification scarcity" paper (26.3% corrective rate) and the Glean figures could not be found or verified
rows.done: All four rules exist: helpers return summaries; the reuse index, knowledge-before-build and design reads before build; about 21 mutation-proven gates, with the standing-red ledger as "break the loop after two"; CLAUDE.md, path rules and the wall. Silent failure is our no-caller and drift classes. One use: test "touches several areas at once" as a reader-selector predictor at the 11 Nov calibration

rows.source: Anthropic, Claude Fable 5.2 (released 9 Nov): the announcement (anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2), the models overview, choosing-a-model, pricing, what's-new and refusals-and-fallback pages. The system card PDF was too large to fetch and is unread
rows.claim: Fable 5.2 beats Opus 5.5 on Anthropic's own table on almost every row (FrontierSWE v2 69.9 against 62.3, Terminal-Bench-Science 74.6 against 58.7, HLE with tools 74.2 against 67.7). At equal quality it costs much less per task: it matches Opus's best FrontierCode at High effort for about half the cost, and its best WANDR at Medium for about 40%. Default effort is `high` against Opus's `medium`. Prices per MTok are double, at $8/$40, with cache reads the same at $0.20. Classifiers refuse cyber, bio and some AI R&D (`frontier_llm`) work; the API answers HTTP 200 with `stop_reason: "refusal"`. API fallback is opt-in and goes only to Opus 4.8 or Opus 5, never Opus 5.5. It is deliberately no better than Opus 5.5 at AI R&D
rows.evidence: Vendor: benchmarks are Anthropic's own, scored at each model's highest effort, and the cost claims compare Fable at low effort with Opus at max. Its own docs say "start with Claude Opus 5.5 for most workloads"
rows.done: Blind test on our own labelled commits, pre-registered before any run (`docs/staging/records/SEAT_PREREG_FABLE_5_2_AGAINST_OPUS_5_5_ON_THE_17_OCT_LABELLED_COMMITS_2026-11-10.md`). Found while setting it up: CLI 2.1.319 does not recognise `claude-fable-5-2` and prices it at Opus rates, so its `total_cost_usd` understates Fable's cost by about half. No change to `model_tier.py` before the test reports
